question: Can a highly parallel, shallow recurrent architecture learn algorithms from short examples and generalize to arbitrarily long inputs?
hypothesis: A convolutional gated recurrent unit applied for n steps over a 2D state (Neural GPU) is easier to train than an NTM and generalizes to much longer inputs.
contributions: Neural GPU architecture based on a convolutional GRU, computationally universal and parallel
First network to learn long binary multiplication that generalizes without error
Parameter sharing relaxation for training deep recurrent networks
Small dropout and gradient noise give large gains in learning and generalization

method.summary: A Neural GPU writes the embedded input into the first column of a [w,n,m] state tensor and applies l stacked convolutional GRU layers for n steps; outputs are read from the first column. Trained with curriculum on binary tasks up to 20 bits (41 for simple tasks), with a 729-run grid search, and tested on lengths up to 2000-4001.
method.task: algorithm learning: binary addition, binary multiplication, copy, reverse, duplicate, count/sort bits

datasets.name: Synthetic binary arithmetic and sequence tasks
datasets.size: 10k random training examples per training length (about 200k total for lengths up to 20)
datasets.split: train on lengths up to 20 bits (up to 41 for simple tasks); test on longer lengths up to 2000 bits (4001 for simple tasks)
datasets.preprocessing: numbers lower-endian binary, equal-length operands zero-padded, sequence length n=2d+1; symbols {0,1,+,PAD} or {0,1,.,PAD}

models.name: LSTM+A
models.architecture: 3-layer LSTM seq2seq with attention, 64 units per cell, as in Vinyals & Kaiser et al. 2015

other.training: original source code, nmax=41, not the authors' regime; run 729 times, best reported

training.objective: softmax over output logits, negative log probability of target
training.optimizer: Adam, epsilon=1e-4, gradient norm clipped to 1
training.lr: grid search over 3 settings (values not stated)
training.dropout: 6%, 9%, 13.5% grid, applied to whole state each step
training.regularisation: gradient noise (Gaussian, std proportional to step^(1/4) -ish: variance inverse to sqrt of step, scaled by noise scale and fraction of non-fully-correct outputs); parameter sharing relaxation; curriculum
training.seeds: 729 grid instances, each with different random seed

other.grid search: 3^6=729 instances over learning rate, initial parameter scale, relaxation pull factor, curriculum progress threshold, gradient noise scale, dropout
other.curriculum: move to d+1 digits after threshold (e.g. over 90% fully correct) on d digits; 20% of minibatches use d uniform in 1..20
other.relaxation: r sets of parameters with pull term toward mean, multiplied by factor at each curriculum step; averaged at max length

inference.decoding: argmax over logits at each output position
inference.samples: best of 729 grid-search models reported; ensembles of 5 averaged outputs mentioned

metrics.name: fraction fully correct
metrics.definition: fraction of test cases for which every bit of the output is correct

eval.protocol: test at lengths 20, 25, 100, 200, 2000 bits; best of 729 runs reported; no significance tests

evidence.quote: we used the Adam optimizer (Kingma & Ba, 2014) with ε = 10−4 and gradients norm clipped to 1

results.claim: A Neural GPU trained on up to 20-bit numbers gets 100% fully correct binary multiplication at 2000 bits
results.setup: bmul@2000, best model of 729-run grid search
results.table: Table 1, row bmul@2000, column Neural GPU

results.quote: Usually only a few of these models generalize to 2000-bit numbers, but a signiﬁcant fraction works well on 200-bit numbers

limits: Only a few of 729 grid-search models generalize to 2000 bits; the reported result is best-of-729
Long decimal multiplication not learned at m=24
Generalization only tested up to about 2000 bits (4001 for simple tasks); technical limits of implementation
No data on natural-language tasks; proposed as future work
stackRNN baseline was not trained with the authors' regime
No learning rates, batch size or step counts given in the paper; defer to released code

train r unshared parameter sets with a pull term toward their mean, increasing the pull during the curriculum

code.snippet: CGRU(s) = u ⊙s + (1 −u) ⊙tanh(U ∗(r ⊙s) + B), where u = σ(U ′ ∗s + B′) and r = σ(U ′′ ∗s + B′′).
